# Naccajātaka (Ja 32)

**ID:** Ja 32
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Naccajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Dancing

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Naccajātaka* (Ja 32) is a narrative in the Pali Jātaka collection (*Ekanipāta*) [Catalog; SuttaCentral]. According to the traditional frame story, the Buddha related this past-life tale while residing at Jetavana, directed at a monk who possessed an excessive number of belongings (*bahubhaṇḍika*); the introductory incident parallels that of the *Devadhammajātaka* [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. In the tale of the past, the King of the Golden Mallards (*haṁsarājā*) convenes an assembly so his daughter may choose a spouse; she selects the peacock, but while dancing exuberantly in celebration, the peacock exposes his hindquarters, displaying shamelessness and immodesty [Anandajoti 2010; Winternitz 1933]. In the *samodhāna*, the Buddha reveals that the shameless peacock was reborn as the monk with many belongings, while the mallard king was the Bodhisatta himself [Fausböll 1877].

The story is attested in early Indian art, appearing on a relief at the 3rd-century BCE Bharhut Stūpa, where an inscription designates it as *Haṁsa-jātaka* (after the Bodhisatta) rather than *Nacca-jātaka* (named after the dance) [Winternitz 1933; Fausböll 1897]. Maurice Winternitz noted that the motif of the dancing peacock—a proverbial Indian emblem of shamelessness—migrated westward via Persia into ancient Greek literature, where Herodotus (VI, 130) incorporated a similar tale into the story of Hippocleides [Winternitz 1933].

According to SuttaCentral, six modern translations exist across four languages, including an English translation by Bhikkhu Sujato [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus records three internal Pali text-reuse matches (spanning 330 characters, longest §0.4–1.4) between the canonical verses and the prose of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Paṭhamo bhāgo), with no cross-language matches scoring 10 or above [DharmaNexus].
